articleHtml:
By David Vance, Senior Financial Modeler & Quantitative Analyst · Last updated: November 27, 2026

What this calculator actually tells you

A mortgage payment is not one number. It is a stack of four: the loan repayment itself (principal and interest), property tax, homeowners insurance, and, when your down payment is small, private mortgage insurance (PMI). Lenders call the full stack PITI. The calculator above adds all four so you see the number your bank account will feel, not the lower figure that advertisements quote.

The sections below go beyond the formula. They show how the payment changes with the term, the rate and extra payments, and how to check whether a payment fits your income before you apply.

Worked example: a $400,000 home, month by month

Take a $400,000 purchase with 20% down ($80,000). The loan is $320,000 at 6.5% for 30 years. Principal and interest come to $2,022.62 per month. Add $400 for property tax and $100 for insurance and the total is $2,522.62.

Look at what the first payment does. The monthly rate is 6.5% ÷ 12 = 0.5417%, so interest for month one is $320,000 × 0.005417 = $1,733.33. Only $289.29 of your $2,022.62 reduces the loan. About 86 cents of every dollar goes to the bank at the start.

That ratio shifts slowly. After 10 years (120 payments) you will have paid roughly $242,700 in principal and interest, yet the balance is still about $271,000. You have repaid only about $48,700 of the original $320,000. Equity in the early years comes mostly from your down payment and from the home rising in value, not from the monthly payments.

15-year vs 30-year: the real trade-off

A shorter term raises the payment but removes a large amount of interest. The table uses the same $320,000 loan and the same 6.5% rate so the comparison is clean. (In practice, 15-year loans usually carry a lower rate than 30-year loans, which widens the gap further.)

TermMonthly P&ITotal interestTotal repaid
30 years$2,022.62≈ $408,100≈ $728,100
15 years$2,787.59≈ $181,800≈ $501,800
Difference+$765−$226,300−$226,300

Paying $765 more each month saves about $226,000 in interest. The catch is flexibility. A 30-year loan lets you choose to pay extra when money is available and fall back to the lower payment when it is not. A 15-year loan forces the higher payment every month.

How much does one percentage point matter?

On the same $320,000, 30-year loan, the rate changes the payment like this:

Interest rateMonthly P&IChange vs 6.5%
5.5%$1,816.93−$205.69
6.5%$2,022.62—
7.5%$2,237.47+$214.85

Each point moves the payment by roughly $205 to $215, or about $75,000 over the life of the loan. This is why comparing offers from three lenders on the same day is worth the effort: a 0.25% difference is real money.

What extra payments do

Add $200 per month to the 6.5% example and the payment becomes $2,222.62. Because the extra goes straight to principal, the loan is cleared in about 280 months (23 years and 4 months) instead of 360. That is roughly 6 years and 8 months sooner, with about $105,000 less interest. Before you do this, confirm your lender applies extra money to principal and does not charge a prepayment penalty. Most conventional loans do not, but check the note.

Will the payment fit your income?

Lenders look at debt-to-income ratio (DTI). A common guideline is the 28/36 rule: housing costs at or below 28% of gross monthly income, and all debts together at or below 36%. Many lenders approve higher ratios, but the guideline is a sensible stress test for yourself.

Using this page's example, a PITI of $2,522.62 at 28% implies a gross income of about $9,009 per month, or roughly $108,100 per year. If your income is below that, the options are a cheaper home, a larger down payment, or a longer term. Remember that car loans, student loans and minimum card payments count toward the 36% limit.

PMI: what it costs and when it ends

If you put down less than 20% on a conventional loan, lenders usually require PMI. Annual cost commonly falls between about 0.3% and 1.5% of the loan amount, depending on credit score and down payment. On a $360,000 loan (10% down on $400,000), 0.5% to 1% is $150 to $300 per month.

On conventional loans you can ask to have PMI removed once the balance reaches 80% of the original home value, and under the U.S. Homeowners Protection Act it must end automatically at 78%. FHA loans follow different rules: with less than 10% down, the mortgage insurance premium often stays for the life of the loan. Compare both options before choosing.

Using this tool for an EMI in India or elsewhere

The principal-and-interest formula is identical worldwide, so you can use the calculator for any currency by ignoring the tax and insurance fields. Example: a ₹50,00,000 loan at 8.5% for 20 years gives an EMI of about ₹43,391. Over 240 months you repay about ₹1.04 crore, which means roughly ₹54.1 lakh is interest. Indian lenders may quote floating rates that reset, so treat the result as an estimate that can change when the benchmark rate moves.

Common mistakes this calculator helps you avoid

  • Entering the home price as the loan amount. Subtract the down payment first.
  • Forgetting closing costs. These are typically 2% to 5% of the loan and are paid on top of the down payment.
  • Leaving out HOA dues. They are not in PITI but do count in your real monthly cost.
  • Assuming tax and insurance stay flat. Both tend to rise; if they are escrowed, your payment rises with them even on a fixed-rate loan.
  • Confusing rate with APR. APR folds in fees and is the fairer number for comparing lenders.
  • Choosing by monthly payment alone. A lower payment from a longer term can cost far more in total interest.

Frequently asked questions

What is the formula for a monthly loan payment?

M = P × [r(1+r)^n] ÷ [(1+r)^n − 1], where P is the loan amount, r is the monthly rate (annual rate ÷ 12) and n is the number of monthly payments. Taxes and insurance are added afterwards as one-twelfth of the annual amounts.

Why is so much of my early payment interest?

Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which is largest at the start. As the balance falls, the interest share shrinks and the principal share grows, even though the total payment stays the same.

Does a bigger down payment always make sense?

It lowers the loan, the interest and possibly PMI. But it also reduces your cash reserve. Many advisers suggest keeping an emergency fund of several months of expenses after closing, even if that means a smaller down payment.

Should I choose a fixed or an adjustable rate?

A fixed rate keeps principal and interest constant for the whole term. An adjustable rate usually starts lower but can rise after the introductory period. Adjustable loans can suit someone who expects to sell or refinance before the reset, but they carry more risk.

Is the result a loan offer?

No. It is an estimate for planning. Your lender's figure will depend on credit history, local taxes, insurance quotes and fees.

How accurate is this calculator?

The principal-and-interest portion uses the standard amortization formula and matches published mortgage tables (for example, $100,000 at 6.5% over 30 years is $632.07 per month). Taxes, insurance and PMI are only as accurate as the values you enter.

Methodology and sources

All figures on this page were calculated with the formula above and rounded to the nearest dollar where marked with ≈. Rates in the tables are illustrations, not current market quotes.
